summary.text:
Read on Q3 2025/26 data, which is the most recent treasury paper we hold, so everything here needs restating from the annual report before it is used. At 31 December 2025 external debt was £795.029m at 3.85%, up from £729.074m, against a full-year CFR indicator of £974.975m. £95m of PWLB EIP loans were drawn over 8 to 12 years at an average 4.86%.

The scale of what is coming is the story. The provisional ten-year plan is £547.7m of gross borrowing — £316.4m General Fund, £231.1m HRA — of which £132.0m is prior-year programme already carried internally. General Fund financing costs are 13.25% of net revenue stream against an average of 7.99% across the 39 authorities in Stoke's own comparison, and the HRA ratio is 29.00%.

The rate assumption is the dated one. In February the report carried Arlingclose's view that Bank Rate would be cut to 3.25% by the middle of 2026. It is 3.75% now and the one-year OIS is about 4.11%. Two internal cautions before anything is sent: the report labels its 31 December figures as certainty rates when they sit at the standard level, and the Appendix 3 interest rate risk actual exceeds its stated limit while the narrative says no limits were breached. Neither belongs in a first contact.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the quarter three treasury report, ahead of Audit and Standards on 15 October. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

One caveat before anything else, because it matters. The most recent Stoke treasury paper we hold is the Q3 report to 31 December 2025, so everything below is on that basis and your annual report will have restated it. If any of it is already out of date, that is our position being stale rather than yours being wrong.

On that basis: external debt was £795.029m at 3.85%, up from £729.074m, with £95m of PWLB EIP loans drawn over eight to twelve years at an average 4.86%. We hold 99 PWLB loans for Stoke at a balance of £791.8m, which is the same book seen from a different date.

The reason we wrote is a single sentence in that report — Arlingclose's view that Bank Rate would be cut to 3.25% by the middle of 2026. Bank Rate is 3.75% today and the market is pricing the one-year at 4.11% and the two-year at 4.21% on the SONIA curve. That is not a criticism of the forecast; forecasts made before the Middle East conflict were overtaken by it across the whole sector, and we have read the same reversal in a dozen reports this summer. It is, though, the clearest possible illustration of why we publish the market-implied path rather than a house view. We do not forecast, deliberately. The implied path is what is actually priced, it updates every day, and it would have shown the divergence as it happened.

That matters here more than in most councils because of what is queued behind it. The provisional ten-year plan is £547.7m of gross borrowing — £316.4m General Fund and £231.1m HRA — of which £132.0m is prior-year programme so far carried internally. General Fund financing costs are already 13.25% of net revenue stream against an average of 7.99% across the 39 authorities in your own comparison, and the HRA ratio is 29.00%. When a programme that size meets a rate assumption, a 50 to 85 basis point difference between assumption and market compounds into real money over ten years.

For the market you would be drawing into: PWLB certainty closed at 4.95% for one year, 5.34% at five, 5.83% at ten and 6.38% at twenty this afternoon on notice 314/26. July's sector lending was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02% — thin, and worth watching when your own plan needs to place several hundred million over a decade. That breakdown, split by HRA and General Fund, is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

One thing from our own data. On the DMO's premature repayment curve today, 57 of the loans we can price sit below par and 41 above, netting to roughly £98.0m of discount on a £791.8m balance. Nothing follows from it: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, only the DMO can quote, and with £547.7m of drawing ahead of you the replacement side plainly dominates anything else. It is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis if it is ever useful.

On training, four fit Stoke. SONIA Forward Curve & OIS and Reading the PWLBpredict are the pair that speak to the rate assumption. HRA treasury & self-financing for the £231.1m HRA half. And The Capital Strategy, which is written for members and is the right frame for a ten-year figure of this size. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
